items.title: The long action and the short action
lines: was / were + -ing = the long action, already going on.
Simple past = the short action that interrupts it.

examples.text: I was walking down the street when it began to rain.

items.title: when changes the story

examples.text: Rita was standing under a tree when it began to rain.
She was already there.
Rita stood under a tree when it began to rain.
Rain came first. Then she moved.

items.tip: Two simple pasts with when → the when-part happens first.

items.title: while and two long actions
lines: while + the long action.
Two long actions at the same time → both -ing.

examples.text: While I was studying in one room, my roommate was having a party.

items.text: I was reading when the phone rang.
items.why: was reading = the long action, already going on.

items.text: At 8 o'clock last night, I ___.
items.why: At an exact time → in progress → was studying.

items.text: When I dropped my cup, the coffee ___ on my lap.
items.why: Drop first, then spill → two simple pasts.

talk.title: A scary night
talk.task: Tell Claude about a scary or surprising night in your life (real or made up).
talk.claudePrompt: You are my English speaking partner. I am practicing the simple past and past progressive by telling a story. Ask me to tell you about a scary or surprising night (real or imaginary). Ask: What were you doing when it started? What happened next? How did you feel? One question at a time.

items.title: Story recipe
lines: Set the scene with was / were + -ing.
Tell the events with the simple past.

examples.text: The sun was shining and birds were singing. Suddenly, a dog ran into the street.

items.why: The long action already going on.

items.why: A series of short events → simple past.

levels.title: Broken plans
levels.full: Unfulfilled Intentions: Was / Were Going To

lines: was / were going to + verb = a plan in the past.
Usually it didn't happen: I was going to call, but I forgot.

examples.text: Jack was going to go to the movie, but he changed his mind.
I was planning to go, but I didn't.

items.ask: Is this a plan or intention?
items.text: I am going to call you at 9:00 tomorrow.
items.why: am going to = a plan for the future.

items.ask: Is this a plan or intention?
items.text: I was going to call you, but I couldn't find your phone number.
items.why: A past plan that didn't happen.

items.ask: Is this a plan or intention?
items.text: I was going to class when I ran into a friend from my childhood.
items.why: was going to class = was walking there.

items.ask: Is this a plan or intention?
items.text: I was planning to go to college right after high school but then decided to work for a year first.
items.why: was planning = a past plan that changed.

items.text: I was going to pay you back for the taxi.
options: I was planning to pay you back.
items.why: was going to = planned, but didn't.

items.text: I was going to stay home on my day off, but I had too much work at the office.
options: I was intending to stay home.
I had a lot of work, but I stayed home.

items.text: Jared was going to the hospital to see his mother when he began to feel ill.
options: Jared was on his way to the hospital.
Jared had plans to see his mother but needed to change them.
Jared didn't go to the hospital.
items.why: was going to the hospital = moving there. We don't know the rest.

items.text: My dad was going to surprise my mom with jewelry for her birthday.
options: He wanted to give her jewelry.
He didn't surprise her with jewelry.
items.why: was going to + verb = planned, but didn't.

items.text: I was going to the train station when I remembered your phone call.
options: I was planning to go to the train station, but I didn't.
I was on my way to the train station.
I didn't go to the train station.
items.why: going to + a place = moving there.

items.text: I was going to get up early this morning, but…
options: I got up at 5:00 as planned.
items.why: was going to → it didn't happen.

items.text: We were hoping to see that movie in a theater, but…
options: we saw it there on Friday.
items.why: were hoping to → it didn't happen.

items.text: I was going to text you, but…
items.why: was going to → it didn't happen.

items.text: We were going to invite Thomas to dinner with us, but…
options: he came and had a great time.
items.why: were going to → the plan failed.

talk.title: Excuses, excuses
talk.task: Finish 'I was going to…, but…' sentences with Claude. Be creative!
talk.claudePrompt: You are my funny English speaking partner. I am practicing 'was / were going to' and 'was planning / hoping to' for plans that didn't happen. Give me the start of a sentence, like 'I was going to call you on your birthday, but…', and I finish it. React with humor, then give the next one. Sometimes ask me to make my own.

items.title: A plan that broke
lines: was / were going to + verb = I had a plan in the past.
Usually the plan didn't happen.

examples.text: Jack was going to go to the movie, but he changed his mind.

items.title: Other ways to say it
lines: These also mean: a plan that didn't happen.

examples.text: I was hoping to go, but I couldn't.

items.title: Plan or on the way?

examples.text: I was going to call you, but I forgot.
I was going to class when I saw Ali.

items.tip: After to: a verb (call) = plan. A place (class) = on the way there.

items.text: I was going to call you.
items.why: was going to → the plan didn't happen.

lines: want, need, decide, can't afford + to + verb.
enjoy, mind, miss, keep, quit + verb-ing.

examples.text: I want to go.
Please keep going.

talk.title: Likes and wants
talk.task: Tell Claude 3 things you enjoy doing and 3 things you want to do this year.
talk.claudePrompt: You are my English speaking partner. I am practicing verbs + to-infinitive (want, need, decide, can't afford) and verbs + -ing (enjoy, mind, miss, keep, quit). Ask me questions that make me use them, like 'What do you enjoy doing on weekends?' or 'What did you decide to do this year?'. One question at a time.

items.title: Two verbs together
lines: After some verbs: to + verb. After others: verb-ing.
There's no easy rule. Learn the groups.

items.title: Side by side

examples.text: I want to go.
Jan decided to wait.
Please keep going.
I enjoy washing dishes.

items.tip: Some take both: It began to rain = It began raining.

items.text: I enjoy ___.
Breakfast is an important meal. [I'm] always eat a big breakfast.
options: I always eat a big breakfast.
I'm always ate a big breakfast.
I always eats a big breakfast.

items.text: While I was working in my office yesterday, my cousin [stops] by to visit me.
options: …my cousin was stop by to visit me.
…my cousin stopped by to visit me.
…my cousin stopping by to visit me.

items.text: Yuki [staied] home because she [catched] a bad cold.
options: Yuki stayed home because she catched a bad cold.
Yuki staied home because she caught a bad cold.
Yuki stayed home because she caught a bad cold.

items.text: My brother [is] looks like our father, but I [am resembling] my mother.
options: My brother looks like our father, but I resemble my mother.
My brother is looking like our father, but I resembling my mother.
My brother look like our father, but I resemble my mother.
items.why: look like and resemble are stative.

items.text: Jun, are you [listen] to me? I am [talk] to you!
options: Jun, do you listen to me? I talk to you!
Jun, are you listening to me? I am talking to you!
Jun, are you listens to me? I am talks to you!

items.text: While I was surfing the Internet yesterday, I [was finding] a really interesting website.
options: …I was found a really interesting website.

items.text: Did you [spoke] English before you [were come] here?
options: Did you speak English before you came here?
Did you speak English before you come here?
Did you spoke English before you came here?

items.text: I [am not] agree with your opinion.
options: I am not agreeing with your opinion.
I don't agree with your opinion.
I not agree with your opinion.
items.why: agree is a verb, not an adjective → don't agree.

items.text: My roommate usually [watch] television, [listen] to music, or [going] out in the evening.
options: My roommate usually watches television, listens to music, or goes out in the evening.
My roommate usually is watching television, listening to music, or going out.
My roommate usually watch television, listens to music, or goes out in the evening.
items.why: Habit, he / she → -s on every verb.

items.text: Right now [Sally in] the kitchen eating breakfast.
options: Right now Sally in the kitchen eats breakfast.
Right now Sally is in the kitchen eating breakfast.
Right now Sally does in the kitchen eating breakfast.
items.why: A sentence needs a verb → is.

items.text: While [I'm driving] home last night, I [heared] a strange noise in the engine.
options: While I drove home last night, I heared a strange noise.
While I was driving home last night, I heard a strange noise in the engine.
While I'm driving home last night, I heard a strange noise in the engine.

items.text: [Why you] talking about me? I'm [not appreciate] that.
options: Why are you talking about me? I don't appreciate that.
Why do you talking about me? I'm not appreciating that.
Why are you talking about me? I'm not appreciate that.
items.why: Question needs are. appreciate is stative.

items.text: Yesterday, while I was sitting at my computer, Shelley [was suddenly coming] into the room.
options: …Shelley was suddenly come into the room.

items.text: I [wasn't knowing] she was there. I was [concentrate] hard on my work.
options: I didn't know she was there. I was concentrating hard on my work.
I wasn't know she was there. I concentrating hard on my work.
I didn't knew she was there. I was concentrated hard on my work.

items.text: When she suddenly [speak], I [am jump]. She [startle] me.
options: When she suddenly spoke, I was jumping. She startles me.
When she suddenly speaks, I jump. She startle me.
When she suddenly spoke, I jumped. She startled me.
items.why: A story in the past → spoke, jumped, startled.
